title: Fight with the fever gone
hookLine: one in the morning, a review doc, two verdicts and one heat: the Gita calls it fever
carry: offer the work; drop ego's fever of 'i did it'
tomorrow: after all that teaching, what does Krishna finally hand Arjuna?

cards: One in the morning. The review doc is open, the screen is the only light, and the face over it is hot. Two verdicts take turns.
I did so much. I did nothing right. Different words, the same heat behind both, the kind that makes a pillow feel warm on both sides.
The Gita has a word for that heat, and it's a plain, bodily one. Fever.

teach.b: In chapter three, Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: offering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free of craving and of the sense of mine, act, and let the fever go.
The Sanskrit is vigatajvara, the fever gone. Jvara is the ordinary word for a fever, the kind a hand on the forehead can feel. A few verses earlier he says where the heat comes from.

teach.h: I AM THE DOER, SAYS EGO.
teach.b: All actions are done by the strands of nature, he says; the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer. That doesn't mean nobody is responsible.
It means an action is bigger than one will: the body that had the strength, the people who showed up, the weather, the bus that came on time.
A fevered review swings between the two verdicts, look what I did, look how I failed, and both put the reviewer in the middle of the story. The cool review asks yesterday's questions honestly.
It owns the mistakes and fixes them. It doesn't take the year's good as a trophy, or its failures as a sentence.
That's why so many Hindus offer their actions to God: some families close a puja by saying everything done is offered to Krishna, Krishnarpanam.
Others hold it more simply, as work handed on to the world.

teach.h: OFFER THE WORK. DROP THE FEVER.
teach.b: Either way, the doer steps a little out of the middle, and the review comes down to a livable temperature: cooler, clearer, kinder.

how: Hindu teachers who draw on Gita 3.27–30 counsel doing one's work wholeheartedly while letting go of the sense of being its only author; many offer each day's work to God, and some families close a puja by offering everything done to Krishna.

o: action owned and reviewed without fever
action that counts only if it's done perfectly
action that burns with guilt until it's fixed

games.q: the cool review — tap the pairs.
p: trophy one minute, sentence the next

s: letting the fever go means not caring what happened
the cool review still owns its mistakes and fixes them; it drops the heat, not the care.
in chapter three, the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer
actions are done by the strands of nature; ego claims them all.
jvara is a word used only for spiritual states
jvara is the ordinary word for a fever.

games.q: your team loses the final, and the captain, your friend, texts: 'it's all on me.' what does Gita chapter three suggest you tell her?
o: agree. owning it fully is the honest thing.
own a fix, but the game was bigger than one will.
blame the referee, so nobody has to feel bad.
games.why: actions are done by many strands, the Gita says; ego thinks, I alone did it. owning a fix is honest. carrying the whole loss is fever.

practice: If there's water near you, hold the glass a moment and feel its coolness in your palm, then take one slow sip and follow the cool down. If there's none, rest the back of a hand against your cheek.
Then breathe, and notice the air cool on the way in and warm on the way out.

wordCard.voice: Karma, without fever: the work owned, its mistakes fixed, offered on, and the doer a little out of the middle.

orig.note: Sanskrit vigatajvara: vigata, gone, and jvara, fever. In Gita 3.30, act with the fever gone.

carryVoice: Your line: offer the work, and drop ego's fever of I did it. One day left in the capstone.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (all actions are done by the gunas of prakriti; one deluded by ego thinks 'I am the doer')
Bhagavad Gita 3.30 (surrendering all actions to me, with mind on the inner self, free from craving and 'mine', fight with the fever gone)
